cues.text: A Marriage the Pope Would Not Annul

By the early 1530s, King Henry VIII of England had grown determined to secure an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, who had failed to provide him a surviving son, so that he might marry Anne Boleyn instead.

Pope Clement VII was unwilling to void a marriage his own predecessor had approved or to offend Catherine's powerful nephew, Emperor Charles V. He repeatedly declined the annulment Henry sought, setting king and papacy on an increasingly bitter collision course.
Cromwell's Legislative Campaign
Henry's chief minister, Thomas Cromwell , orchestrated a sustained legislative campaign through Parliament across 1533 and 1534.
It systematically stripped the papacy of its traditional authority over the English Church by transferring the right to appoint bishops to the crown and ending papal fees and annates.
In early 1533, he had Archbishop Thomas Cranmer independently declare Henry's marriage to Catherine void and his marriage to Anne, already secretly performed, valid.
Cromwell's methods extended well beyond formal legislation.
He oversaw a deliberate and sustained propaganda campaign of sermons and pamphlets attacking papal authority throughout the kingdom.
By the time Parliament was asked to vote on the Act itself, English public opinion had already been carefully prepared to receive it.
Supreme Head on Earth
The Act of Supremacy itself was passed by Parliament in November 1534.
It formally declared Henry and his successors "the only supreme head in earth of the Church of England."
It granted them full authority to correct and reform errors, heresies, and abuses within it.
This language claimed for the English crown powers the Catholic Church had always reserved to the papacy alone.
A companion Treason Act made it a capital offense to deny the king's new title by any means, spoken or written.
A Test of Conscience
The Act forced every English subject of consequence to choose between loyalty to the crown and loyalty to Rome.
Most conformed outwardly, while a determined minority refused outright.
St. Thomas More , the former Lord Chancellor, and St. John Fisher , Bishop of Rochester, both declined the required oath.
They were executed for treason in 1535, becoming the most prominent of what would grow into a long line of English Catholic martyrs across the following century and a half.
More's own reasoning, recorded from his trial, remains among the clearest Catholic statements of conscience against royal supremacy ever preserved.
He could not deny the authority of the pope, he said, without jeopardizing his own soul to perpetual damnation, whatever the cost that refusal carried in this life.
A Rupture, Not Yet a Reformation
Henry's own theological convictions remained, for most of his reign, substantially Catholic in content, even as he rejected papal authority in structure.
The Act of Supremacy was, at its origin, less a doctrinal revolution than an assertion of royal jurisdiction.
Yet it opened the door through which more thoroughgoing Protestant reform would enter England under his son Edward VI and, more lastingly, under his daughter Elizabeth I.
Legacy

Briefly repealed under the Catholic Mary I in 1554 and restored in modified form by Elizabeth I in 1559, the Act of Supremacy established the constitutional foundation on which the Church of England has stood ever since.
It permanently severed the English Church's structural bond with Rome after nearly a thousand years of shared communion.
What began as one king's determination to secure a male heir reshaped, in the end, the religious map of an entire nation.

The martyrs it produced — More, Fisher, and the many who followed them to the scaffold rather than deny the pope's authority — remain the Catholic Church's most enduring witness against the claim the Act itself had tried to establish.
